title: Logistic regression
dek: Bernoulli or binomial likelihood, logit link: ℓ(β) = ∑ [ y xᵀβ − log(1+e^{xᵀβ}) ]. Coefficients are log odds ratios in that mean model.
story: Write Yᵢ ~ Bernoulli(πᵢ), logit πᵢ = xᵢᵀβ. The likelihood is the product π^y (1−π)^{1−y}. That is the whole model. Everything else — odds ratios, ROC plots, p-values — is a reading of this likelihood or a different target grafted onto it.
exp(β_k) multiplies the odds π/(1−π), not the risk π, unless π is small enough that odds ≈ risk. In pulmonary TB, smear-positivity is not rare; do not caption an odds ratio as a risk ratio.

Complete separation (a covariate perfectly predicts y) drives |β̂| → ∞ and IRLS weights to 0. That is an infinite MLE, not a huge effect you should publish as 400.0. Penalisation or a prior is the statistical response; “drop the covariate” is a scientific decision.
deepTitle: Likelihood, OR vs RR, and sparse events
deep: Log-likelihood: ℓ(β) = ∑ᵢ { yᵢ ηᵢ − log(1+e^{ηᵢ}) } with η = xᵀβ (no extra φ). Score: Xᵀ(y − π) = 0. At the MLE, predicted frequencies match observed totals in the column space of X — the exponential-family mean match.

Risk ratio from a logit model is a function of x, not a single exp(β). If you want a risk ratio or risk difference as the scientific parameter, fit a log or identity binomial (checking that μ stays in range) or report derived predictions.
Rare events: Firth penalty, exact methods, or a weakly informative prior on β. Wald intervals on huge β̂ are theatre. Profile or posterior intervals keep the shape of ℓ.
Clustered binary data: the Bernoulli product is wrong. Use a mixed logit, GEE with sandwich, or a survey design. An LRT that ignores clustering is anti-conservative.

formulas.label: Odds ratio
formulas.note: Holds for a 0/1 covariate under this mean model, adjusted for the other columns of X.

visual.caption: Logistic mean as a sigmoid on the η scale: three linear predictors (HIV−/HIV+/cavitary) shift π without ever leaving (0,1). The curves are sampling laws of a latent sketch; the scientific object is π(x) = logit⁻¹(xᵀβ).

example.title: Odds ratio for cavitation
example.setup: n = 200 TB cases, Y = smear-positive. β̂_cav = 0.693, se = 0.28, adjusted for HIV and days of cough. Interpret and test.

steps.title: OR
steps.body: exp(0.693) ≈ 2.00. Adjusted odds of smear-positivity are about twice as high with cavitation, in this mean model.

steps.title: Interval on a better scale
steps.body: Wald on β: 0.693 ± 1.96×0.28 ≈ (0.14, 1.24). Exponentiate: OR interval ≈ (1.15, 3.46). Do not form 2.00 ± 1.96×(2.00×0.28) and pretend it is as good.

steps.title: LRT cousin
steps.body: Drop cavitation, compare ℓ. If n is not tiny, Wald and LRT will agree. If cavitation is rare, prefer the LRT or a profile interval.

example.takeaway: Write the Bernoulli likelihood, quote OR as exp(β), and refuse to rename it a risk ratio when π is not small.

check.prompt: An odds ratio from a logit GLM equals a risk ratio when:
choices: Approximately when the outcome is rare, or exactly only in special designs/limits — not in general at moderate π
check.answer: Approximately when the outcome is rare, or exactly only in special designs/limits — not in general at moderate π
check.why: Odds = π/(1−π). If π is small, 1−π ≈ 1 and OR ≈ RR. Smear-positivity is often not rare.

whyWrong.Always, by invariance: Invariance maps MLEs, it does not make OR = RR.
whyWrong.When n>30: Sample size is not the issue.

check.prompt: Intercept-only logit, 30 successes in 100 trials. MLE of π is 0.3. MLE of β₀ = logit(π) is closest to:
On the density plate the three curves sit at different means but stay as proper densities. The logistic lesson is:
check.figureHint: Three profiles labelled with different π.
choices: The linear predictor can shift π without leaving (0,1), unlike an unconstrained identity mean
Odds ratios are visible as areas under the curve
The rightmost curve is a prior
check.answer: The linear predictor can shift π without leaving (0,1), unlike an unconstrained identity mean
check.why: The sigmoid mean is the point. The cartoon densities are schematic, not the Bernoulli pmf itself.

whyWrong.Odds ratios are visible as areas under t: OR comes from β, not from those areas.
whyWrong.The rightmost curve is a prior: All three are schematic sampling profiles.
